steps.label: Plan and Build Your Own Game
steps.content:
Year 6 Scratch

Plan and Build Your Own Game

Year 6, 6.2.5

  • Pick a kind of game and plan it.
  • Build it one piece at a time, testing as you go.
  • Make it feel good to play: sound, a score on the stage, sprites that react.

steps.label: A Plan Before Code
steps.content:
A Plan Before Code

Here is the plan for Fruit Catcher, the catching game you have built. Yours will have the same parts.

Think → Pair → ShareWhy plan first? What goes wrong if you start with no plan?Show the answer

You know what to build next, and you can test each part against the plan. With no plan you guess, and the game often has no way to win or lose.

Fruit Catcher plan

  • Sprites: Bowl (the player moves it), Apple (falls from a random place).
  • Controls: left and right arrow keys.
  • Variables: score (apples caught), lives (misses left, starts at 3).
  • Win or lose: lose when lives reaches 0.
  • Each line of the plan becomes a script or a sprite.
  • Build one line at a time.
  • Test it before the next line.

steps.label: Check: The Plan
steps.content:
Check: The Plan

Use the Fruit Catcher plan.

items.prompt: In the Fruit Catcher plan, what is lives?
items.explain: lives stores a number that changes while the game runs, so it is a variable.

items.prompt: You add 6 new blocks at once and the game breaks. Why is testing after each small change better?
options: You know the bug is in the part you just added
items.explain: Testing each small change means a new bug must be in the few blocks you just added.

steps.label: Pick Your Game
steps.content:
Pick Your Game

Each game comes with its sprites, sounds and backdrops. You write all the code.

Think → Pair → ShareLook at the four games. What does every one of them need: a control, a variable, a way to win or lose?Show the answer

All four. Catch and Dodge move a sprite with the arrow keys, Maze moves the Hero, Pop uses clicks. Each counts something (score, lives, keys, time) and each ends: lives run out, the Door opens, or time runs out.

Catch

Move the Bowl.

Catch Apples, miss Rocks.

Dodge

Steer the Ship.

Dodge Meteors, grab Stars.

Maze

Walk the Hero.

Get the Key, avoid the Ghost.

Pop

Click the Balloons.

Score before time runs out.

Or pick My own idea: one sprite and an empty stage.

steps.label: Plan: Your Game
steps.content:
Plan: Your Game

Short answers are fine. Keep this slide open while you build.

Think → Pair → ShareWhy write down how the game ends before you build it?Show the answer

The ending decides which variable you need and what the if block checks, for example lives = 0 or time = 0.

Game

Which game? What is it called?

Controls

Which keys or clicks?

Variable

What does it count? What does the green flag set it to?

Win or lose

How does the game end?

steps.label: Activity 1: Build Your Game
steps.content:
Activity 1: Build Your Game

Work on your own. Open My Game and pick the game you planned.

Build it

  • Controls first. Test them.
  • Then a loop that keeps the game running.
  • Then a variable: set it at the green flag, change it during the game.
  • Then an if block and a way to win or lose.

The panel beside TurboWarp lists the checks. Press Check my project as often as you like: it plays your game and tells you what it saw.

steps.label: Make It Feel Good
steps.content:
Make It Feel Good

When every check passes, make the game fun to play. The bonus checks look for these.

Think → Pair → ShareTwo games score the same way. One plays a sound and the sprite grows when you score. Which feels better to play? Why?Show the answer

The one with sound and movement. The player sees and hears that they scored straight away, so it feels like a reward.

if <touching [Ship v] ?> then
start sound [coin v]
change [score v] by (1)
change size by (10)
end
  • Sound: start sound when you score or get hit.
  • Score on the stage: tick the box next to the variable.
  • React: change size, a colour effect or a costume.
  • Level 2: switch to the Level 2 backdrop with a broadcast.

steps.label: Activity 2: Make It Feel Good
steps.content:
Activity 2: Make It Feel Good

Work on your own. Open My Game again: your project is still there.

Build it

  • Add a sound.
  • Show the score on the stage.
  • Make a sprite react when you score.
  • Add Level 2. Make it harder.

The panel beside TurboWarp lists the checks. Press Check my project as often as you like: it plays your game and tells you what it saw.

steps.label: Arcade: Play Each Other's Games
steps.content:
Arcade: Play Each Other's Games

Leave your game open. Move to the next computer when your teacher says.

Think → Pair → ShareAfter playing: which game was most fun? What made it fun?Show the answer

Answers vary. Look for clear controls, sound, a score you can see, and a game that gets harder.

At each game

  • Click the green flag. Play for two minutes.
  • Try every control.
  • Try to win, and try to lose.

Tell the maker

  • One thing that was fun.
  • One thing that did not work, if you found one.
